overview.title: 📖 Overview: Names, Languages, and Where Intent Ends
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 13a–13b
overview.hebrewSource: שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ ה׳ אֶחָד — עַד כָּאן צְרִיכָה כַּוָּונַת הַלֵּב, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The first chapter closes by finishing the Sages' answer to Ben Zoma: 'Israel' becomes primary and 'Jacob' secondary, just as later troubles make earlier ones forgotten. That leads to the renaming of Abram and Sarai and whether calling Abraham 'Abram' is a transgression. The second chapter opens with a mishna on reading Shema with intent, greeting people between and within paragraphs, and why the three portions are ordered as they are. The Gemara asks whether mitzvot require intent, records the dispute over reciting Shema in Hebrew or any language, and then works through a sequence of baraitot about how much of Shema needs intent — concluding with Rabbi Meir's view, endorsed by Rava, that the first verse is what matters. Stories about Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's one-verse Shema and about falling asleep after it show that principle in practice.

slides.title: 📛 Three Renamings, Three Different Rules
slides.subtitle: The Gemara moves from 'Israel is primary, Jacob secondary' to the names of Abraham and Sarah
rows: First father (אָב) of Aram only; finally father of the whole world — 'father of a multitude of nations' (Gen. 17:5)
Bar Kappara: transgresses a positive mitzva ('your name will be Abraham'); Rabbi Eliezer: a negative one ('shall no longer be called Abram')
First princess of her own nation; finally princess of the whole world
No transgression — the command 'do not call her Sarai' (Gen. 17:15) was said to Abraham alone, not as a general rule
Israel primary, Jacob secondary — 'Do not remember the former events' (Isa. 43:18): the kingdoms' subjugation eclipses even the Exodus
Permitted — Scripture itself reverts: 'And God said to Israel… Jacob, Jacob' (Gen. 46:2)

callout.label: Objection and answer:
callout.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin: Nehemiah 9:7 says 'Who chose Abram'! Answer: there the prophet is recounting God's praises from the beginning — what the situation was originally, before the name was changed. Rav Yosef adds that 'Behold, I do a new thing' is the war of Gog and Magog, like the traveler who forgot the wolf and the lion once the snake had come.

slides.title: 🗣️ Shema in Hebrew Only, or in Any Language?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and the Rabbis each have a verse — and each must explain the other's

lines.speaker: Rabbi
lines.text: Shema must be recited as it is written (כִּכְתָבָהּ). 'And these words… shall be' (Deut. 6:6) — בַּהֲוָיָיתָן יְהוּ, as they are they shall remain.

lines.speaker: Rabbis
lines.text: In any language. 'Hear (שְׁמַע), Israel' — in any language that you hear and understand.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Then what does Rabbi do with 'Hear'? — Let your ears hear what your mouth utters: recite audibly. And the Rabbis? They follow the view that one who did not make it audible still fulfilled his obligation.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: And what do the Rabbis do with 'shall be'? — That one may not recite Shema out of order (לְמַפְרֵעַ). Rabbi learns that from 'the words' rather than 'words'; the Rabbis do not expound that extra letter.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Does this mean Rabbi holds the whole Torah may be read in any language, so a special verse was needed for Shema? Not necessarily — 'shall be' was needed to counter 'Hear'. And the Rabbis, that the whole Torah must be Hebrew? Not necessarily — 'Hear' was needed to counter 'shall be'.

callout.label: Note:
callout.text: Each side's verse is 'necessary' only because the other side's verse exists, so neither view can be extended to Torah reading in general.

slides.title: 🎯 How Much of Shema Requires Intent?
slides.subtitle: From 'mitzvot require intent' to Rabbi Meir's first verse

nodes.content: ❓ Mishna: one reading the Torah when the time for Shema arrives fulfils it 'if he focused his heart'. Does this prove mitzvot require intent?
🚫 No — 'focused his heart' may mean intent to read. But he is already reading! — He is reading to proofread the text (לְהַגִּיהַּ), so intent to read the words is all that is needed

📜 Baraita: 'These words… upon your heart' — 'these' limits intent to the first paragraph (Rabbi Eliezer). Rabbi Akiva: 'which I command you this day, upon your heart' — the whole paragraph requires intent. Rabbi Yoḥanan: halakha like Rabbi Akiva

columns.label: Rav Zutra
columns.content: First paragraph: intent and recitation; from there on, recitation without intent

columns.label: Rabbi Yoshiya
columns.content: First paragraph: recitation and intent; from there on, intent without recitation ('to speak of them' there refers to teaching Torah)

columns.label: R' Aḥa (R' Yehuda)
columns.content: Once he focused his heart in the first paragraph, no more is needed — Rabbi Yoḥanan rules like him

nodes.content: ✅ Rabbi Meir: 'Hear, Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One' — intent of the heart is required to here. Rava: the halakha follows Rabbi Meir

callout.label: Related:
callout.text: Rav Yehuda: recite until 'upon your heart' standing in one place; Rabbi Yoḥanan: the whole first paragraph — consistent with his ruling like Rabbi Aḥa. Rabbi Yitzḥak uses 'and you shall place these words' for tefillin of the arm opposite the heart.

slides.title: 😴 The First Verse in Practice
slides.subtitle: Stories and rulings that turn Rabbi Meir's principle into daily conduct

steps.content: 1️⃣ Sumakhos: whoever lengthens Eḥad has his days and years lengthened. Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov: in the dalet. Rav Ashi: provided he does not rush the ḥet
2️⃣ Rabbi Yirmeya saw Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba lengthening greatly: 'Once you have crowned Him above, below and in the four directions, you need no more'
3️⃣ 'Shema Yisrael…' — this was Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's Shema. Rav never saw him accept the yoke of Heaven; Rabbi Ḥiyya: when he passes his hands over his face in the lesson, that is his Shema
4️⃣ Did Rabbi complete it later? Bar Kappara: no — that is why he sought a lesson mentioning the Exodus. Rabbi Shimon his son: yes — and he still mentioned the Exodus 'at its time'

5️⃣ Rav: said the first verse and was overcome by sleep — he has fulfilled his obligation. Rav Naḥman to his servant Daru: 'for the first verse trouble me; beyond that, do not'. Rabba likewise strove only for the first verse

6️⃣ Rav Yosef: one lying flat on his back (פְּרַקְדָּן) may not recite Shema. Sleeping so, leaning slightly, is allowed; reciting, even leaning, is not — Rabbi Yoḥanan did so only because he was corpulent

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: The verse of God's unity is the core of accepting Heaven's kingship; the rest is recitation whose lapse does not undo the mitzva.

slides.title: 🤝 Greeting Someone in the Middle of Shema
slides.subtitle: The mishna's two positions, and the Gemara's repair of its wording

boxes.title: Rabbi Meir
items: Between paragraphs: greet out of respect (כָּבוֹד) — and needless to say, respond
Within a paragraph: greet out of fear (יִרְאָה) — and needless to say, respond
As written, 'respond' seemed redundant, and the two views collapsed into one; the Gemara says the mishna is incomplete (חַסּוֹרֵי מְחַסְּרָא) and restores it

boxes.title: Rabbi Yehuda
items: Within a paragraph: greet out of fear, respond out of respect
Between paragraphs: greet out of respect, respond to any person
Also: between VaYomer and Emet VeYatziv one may not interrupt at all

callout.label: The breaks:
callout.text: Between the first and second blessing; the second blessing and Shema; Shema and VeHaya im Shamoa; VeHaya im Shamoa and VaYomer; VaYomer and Emet VeYatziv. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa: Shema comes first to accept the yoke of Heaven before the yoke of mitzvot; VeHaya im Shamoa precedes VaYomer because it applies day and night, while tzitzit applies only by day.

summary.principle: Names, languages, and intent all follow the same logic — the essential core (Israel over Jacob, the first verse of Shema) is what must be fixed, while the rest may be secondary.

flowSteps.content: 🐺 'No longer Jacob' means Israel primary, Jacob secondary — later troubles eclipse earlier ones; Abram may not be used, Sarai and Jacob may
📜 Chapter 2 mishna: intent while reading Torah; greetings between and within paragraphs; the order of the three portions
🗣️ Rabbi: Shema in Hebrew ('shall be'); Rabbis: any language ('Hear') — each verse needed only because of the other

columns.content: 🎯 Rabbi Akiva / Rabbi Aḥa: intent for the whole first paragraph (Rabbi Yoḥanan)
🎯 Rabbi Meir: intent only through 'the Lord is One' — Rava rules so

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: The first verse is the acceptance of Heaven's kingship — Rabbi's one-verse Shema, lengthening Eḥad, and falling asleep after it all rest on this

quiz.q: Why is one who calls Sarah 'Sarai' not in violation, while one who calls Abraham 'Abram' transgresses according to bar Kappara and Rabbi Eliezer?
o: Because Sarah's name change was never recorded in the Torah
Because the instruction about Sarai was addressed to Abraham alone, whereas Abraham's renaming is stated in general terms
Because women's names are not subject to such rules
Because Scripture later reverts and calls her Sarai
quiz.e: The Gemara answers that God said to Abraham specifically 'you shall not call her name Sarai' (Genesis 17:15), while 'your name shall no longer be called Abram' is general. Jacob is different because Scripture itself later calls him 'Jacob, Jacob' (Genesis 46:2).

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, what does the word 'Hear' (Shema) in Deuteronomy 6:4 teach?
o: That Shema may be recited in any language one understands
That one must not recite Shema out of order
That one should make one's ears hear what one's mouth utters
That the whole Torah must be read in Hebrew
quiz.e: Rabbi uses 'and they shall be' for Hebrew-only recitation, and 'Hear' to require audible recitation. The Rabbis use 'Hear' for any language and hold that inaudible recitation still fulfils the obligation.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara deflect the proof that 'mitzvot require intent' from the mishna about reading Torah when Shema's time arrives?
o: It says the mishna follows Beit Shammai
It explains the reader was proofreading the text, so 'focused his heart' means intent to read the words, not intent to fulfil a mitzva
It says the reader had already recited Shema earlier
It says the mishna refers only to the evening Shema
quiz.e: The Gemara suggests the case is one reading to emend the text (בְּקוֹרֵא לְהַגִּיהַּ); such a person needs only intent to read, so no proof about intent for mitzvot can be drawn.

quiz.q: What does Rabbi Meir hold about intent in Shema, and who rules in accordance with him?
o: The entire first paragraph requires intent; Rabbi Yoḥanan rules so
Intent is required only through 'the Lord is One'; Rava rules so
All three paragraphs require intent; Rabbi Akiva rules so
No intent is required at all; Rav Yosef rules so
quiz.e: The baraita states that intent of the heart is required until 'Hear, Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One' — the statement of Rabbi Meir — and Rava says the halakha follows Rabbi Meir.

quiz.q: What instruction did Rav Naḥman give his servant Daru about Shema?
o: Wake me for the entire Shema even if I have fallen asleep
Trouble me to recite the first verse; beyond that, do not trouble me
Never wake me once I have lain down
Recite Shema on my behalf if I fall asleep
quiz.e: Following Rav's ruling that one who recited the first verse and was overcome by sleep fulfilled his obligation, Rav Naḥman told Daru to bother him only for the first verse.
